name: Google Compute Engine A3 / A3 Ultra (NVIDIA H100 and H200)
region: us-central1 (prices as published); a3 and a3-ultragpu offered across us-east1/4/5, us-west, europe-west, asia-northeast
price_basis: per GPU-hour. a3-highgpu-8g = 8x H100 at $88.490000119/instance-hr / 8 = $11.0613. a3-megagpu-8g = 8x H100 at $93.400712807/8 = $11.6751. a3-ultragpu-8g = 8x H200 at $84.806908493/8 = $10.6009. Prices are the us-central1 column as published 2026-10-03. PRICE CLASS: this is a PUBLISHED LIST PRICE - an asking rate a new customer is quoted, not a realised, discounted or negotiated transaction rate. A real bill is at or below this and typically well below it once commitments, credits and committed-use discounts are applied.
notes:
THE MOST EXPENSIVE ON-DEMAND H100 HOUR IN THE ENTIRE SLICE - $11.06/GPU-hour against $3.29 for the cheapest single H100 (Lambda) and $6.88 for AWS on-demand. Two caveats that cut the other way. First, the page's 1-year and 3-year CUD columns for a3-highgpu-8g render in an order that makes the 1-year figure ($61.38) look HIGHER than a plausible on-demand relationship and the 3-year figure ($38.86) far lower; the column ordering in the rendered table is ambiguous, so treat the CUD numbers as suspect and only the on-demand column as solid. Second, Google states accelerator-optimized machines are NOT eligible for sustained use discounts or flexible committed use discounts - only resource-based CUDs apply. So the discount path on A3 is narrower than the headline suggests. Regional spread is not visible in this page: the region selector ships with us-central1 preselected and requesting ?region=us-east4 returned byte-identical figures, so the page did not honour the parameter server-side and no regional comparison should be drawn from it. Access requires a reservation in practice, not just quota: A3 capacity has historically been allocation-only. Important structural note: the on-demand price is bundled with vCPU, RAM AND bundled Local SSD (a3-highgpu-8g carries 6,000 GiB), which is why the per-GPU figure looks bad next to a bare neocloud GPU - you are not paying for a GPU alone.

 EXPORT CONTROL (2026-10-04, mechanism-level; sources spl-bis-2026-05-d5-guidance, spl-bis-2026-01-advanced-computing-case-by-case): renting capacity does NOT remove the export-control question, it relocates it. Providing remote access to controlled computing capability can constitute a transfer under the EAR, so the provider must screen the end user; and separately, under the 91 FR 1684 licence regime the consignee must run KYC procedures to prevent unauthorized remote access and must manage and limit IaaS access to the hardware - obligations pushed onto the customer, who must be told to implement them. For a customer headquartered or parented in Country Group D:5 or Macau the 742.6(a)(6)(iii)(A) end-user/parent test can bite even when the capacity is consumed in a permitted region. Recorded true because the underlying hardware is controlled and the provider carries the screening duty, not because access to a US region is itself restricted.

 LEAD TIME: null, and correct as null. For a listed on-demand instance type the provisioning delay is effectively zero - capacity is allocated per request - so a week count would be meaningless; the real gate for scarce shapes is either a quota increase or a capacity reservation, not a lead time. Where a published commitment horizon exists it IS recorded: AWS documents that a Capacity Block may be reserved with a start time up to EIGHT WEEKS in the future (source spl-aws-capacity-block-booking-horizon), which is a floor on how far ahead scarce capacity must be committed, not a wait. On-demand and Spot tiers publish no lead time at all; their constraint is availability, and the repo records that as availability=in-stock or a spot/reality note rather than as a fabricated week figure. Probe log in source spl-negative-no-oem-publishes-lead-time.
